title: How Far It Can Go and How Hot It Gets: The Energy of the Way Home, the Computer That Never Sleeps, and a Slope That Is Fine for a Minute

questions.question: Why is the computer part of the energy of a route?
options: It draws power all the time, for as long as the route takes
It makes the motors less efficient
Its weight adds to the rolling resistance
It is not: only the motors draw from the battery
questions.explanation: The computer and sensors drew 8 W the whole time. On tarmac at 1 m/s that was 79 percent of the 10.1 J each metre cost.

questions.question: A metre of sand cost, against a metre of tarmac:
options: 10.1 J against 22.0 J
22.0 J for both: the computer dominates
79 J against 10.1 J
22.0 J against 10.1 J
questions.explanation: Sand's rolling resistance is several times tarmac's, so the motors' share grows while the computer's 8 J a metre stays the same.

questions.question: The vehicle that took the way home as flat turned back at 16.8 m and was:
options: Home with 71 J to spare
25 J short of getting home
Home with nothing to spare
Stopped at the turn, with no way back
questions.explanation: It priced the return as flat ground and went too far. The one that priced the return over the sand turned at 12.0 m and got home with 71 J.

questions.question: A slope of 20 degrees reached the motor's limit in:
options: Never: it settled under the limit
questions.explanation: The steady temperature at 20 degrees is over the 75 K limit, so there is a time, 62 s. At 14 degrees it settled at 71 K.

questions.question: What does the closed form of the time to the limit say when the steady rise is under the limit?
options: The limit is reached at once
A time longer than the route
Never: it settles below the limit
A negative time, which is an error
questions.explanation: The winding settles at the power times the thermal resistance. If that is under the limit, the limit is never reached.

questions.question: Why does speed matter twice for the energy of a route?
options: Air drag grows with the square of the speed
The work is the same and the computer runs for longer at a lower speed
The motors are less efficient when fast
Faster wheels slip more
questions.explanation: The work against the ground depends on the distance. The 8 W of electronics is paid by the second, so a slower run of the same route costs more.
